acceptance: One registered root lists and reads without exposing its Git metadata or links, and nothing outside it nor another folder is reached; a missing name inside it is not_found while a name behind a link says nothing (invalid_path). Writes need the revision they replace (or say they create), and two writes from the same revision cannot both land. Every request checks the folder's grant as it is now: read-only refuses writing, making and removing, and a revoked share refuses even reading. Changes made on this computer arrive as coalesced watch events; a two-second metadata reconcile names what the system's events missed on every platform and ends with its folder; a stopped watch scans and publishes nothing. A directory swapped for a link to outside between its check and its use is never read, listed, removed, written or made into through. The shared conformance cases of host-file-protocol-v1 all hold.

A directory of exactly 10,000 entries lists in order well inside the gateway's timeout and one more is refused (too_many_entries); files read back byte for byte with their revision up to 8 MiB and not past it (unsupported_file); a binary write lands unchanged.

File operations go inside the folder's own SSH session as the protocol's typed requests (Git as named operations); a folder that is not an ID is refused. A read is asked again through a lost connection, on a new one; a write is sent exactly once. Failures keep their code and status (an offline computer, a refused tunnel with the Cloud's reason). A watch delivers changes, reports the computer offline, rescans after reconnecting, and ends for good on a definite denial.

A folder on another computer is a workspace with its own identity and no local path: it lists and reads through that computer, saves with the revision it replaces, and on a rejected compare-and-swap shows the other computer's version without replaying the save; a write whose outcome is unknown is sent once and the draft stays. It creates, renames and deletes only inside the folder and only when editable. Its reachability is worded for the person (offline with the computer's name); a change hands the workbench only the paths it names (a rescan drops everything), and a changed session ends what was admitted under the old one.

reason: TS's device data port runs mutations to unrelated paths concurrently and only keeps overlapping ones in order. The native remote folder sends its changes one at a time, in the order they were made (one mutation lane per folder), so an unrelated change waits for the one before it; order is kept either way.

acceptance: A remote folder's identity is one per account, device, folder and deployment, the same however the deployment is written; anything that is not an ID, an address outside the PuppyOne family or one carrying credentials is refused, and so is a path out of the folder.

This computer's device key is created once per account, its private half kept in the keychain (only public parts on disk); a lost registration reply registers the same key again, and a registered device is not registered twice. It signs as the Cloud checks, with nobody signed in, and only for its own account's device; another account here never reuses it, and a non-ID account is refused. Forgetting another account's device leaves it; forgetting it after a revocation takes its key, and a later share registers a new one.

reason: TS can run the host on Linux with Electron's secret storage and must refuse its plaintext fallback. The native host keeps device keys only in the macOS login keychain; there is no Linux secret-storage backend, so there is no plaintext fallback to refuse.

acceptance: On macOS the host starts at login from a per-user LaunchAgent that runs this installation's own program with --puppyone-host (escaped for the plist), which is removed when turned off and reported as on only while it is this installation's, unchanged; the setting is a yes or no.

reason: TS writes an XDG autostart entry on Linux and an App login item on Windows. The native host's login entry is a macOS LaunchAgent only; elsewhere starting at login is reported as unsupported.

acceptance: The App reaches its host over a control socket in a directory only this user can read (0700, socket and token 0600), and only a client that presents the token is answered; the host borrows the App's person for its Cloud calls, and only for its own device and folder routes; observers may read and never change.

reason: TS's control channel carries a failure's HTTP status and code to the App. The native App and host are one program and the App never branches on a host failure's code, so the native channel carries the failure's message only.

acceptance: Outside the rollout a login entry an earlier build wrote starts nothing; the host's state and lock live in its own directory under the App's data for its channel, never the App's profile itself; a second host for the same App leaves the one already serving alone.

A shared folder keeps one canonical local mapping under one ID, which a lost reply registers again, and the Cloud is never told its path; it is this owner's alone (another account or device resolves nothing). Running things stays off until this computer allows it and only for an editable folder; narrowing to view-only ends every permission to run, and widening back gives editing only. A link or Git metadata is never a root, and a retry with other settings is refused. Removing denies here first and asks the Cloud again after a lost reply; a revoked device loses every folder here without a word to the Cloud.

Host operations stay off outside the rollout. Sharing belongs to the host: registering a folder needs this computer's explicit yes (and an answer given under another sign-in changes nothing), runs the person's Cloud calls through the App, keeps the device key and the folder's path with the host, continues after the App quits and resumes by itself after a restart. A pause stops it and outlives a restart with every folder kept. Signing out here stops it across restarts; someone else signing in does not resume it, the owner does. Running things is asked about separately, and where there is no sandbox nothing runs and there is no unsandboxed way. The host runs only host routes with the person's session, for this deployment.

reason: TS asks with a native message box and then re-checks that the folder is still the workspace assigned to the asking window. The native sharing dialog is opened for one folder chosen on the Homepage, not for the window's workspace, so there is no assigned workspace that could change under the question.

TS withdraws a share whose folder has gone from disk once its project is found elsewhere (only that share, telling the Cloud, asking nobody). The native App does not retire such a share: it stays registered and the host serves nothing for it (root_changed) until it is stopped from the App.

acceptance: Recent folders on other computers are remembered by ID and name per account, newest first, with the last one open.

Another computer reaches a shared folder only over SSH with the Cloud's certificate for this device: another device's, another account's, an expired one, one with critical options or from another authority are refused, as is a login for a folder other than the tunnel's and a host whose key is not the device's registered key. Inside, the file protocol works (list, read, conditional write, conflict, watch) as the folder is granted, so view-only writes are refused on the host itself. A terminal runs only with this computer's consent, with a pty, and reports its exit; one command runs binary safe with its exit status, and nothing runs without consent; a session that fails to start ends on its own and the host keeps serving. There is no SFTP or port forwarding, and sessions end when the folder stops being shared; consent changed here applies to the open connection. A refused tunnel says the Cloud's reason; an unanswered read times out and an unanswered write is uncertain; a connection that ends is replaced on the next request.
